analysis.one_liner: Creates a private-sector-led task force to fast-track repeal of federal regulations that burden businesses.
analysis.headline: The LIBERATE Act never left committee: introduced April 7, 2022 with 6 Republican cosponsors, it died without a vote when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a task force, made up mostly of private-sector members appointed by congressional leaders, to identify federal regulations that burden U.S. industries. Its repeal recommendations would go to Congress as special messages, and any joint resolution to repeal the listed rules would get a fast-track process: committees discharged after 25 days, limited debate, no amendments, and Senate points of order waived [S2] [S3]. The bill died in committee with no action beyond its initial referral [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses subject to federal regulation would gain if the bill passed. The task force would target rules that raise operating costs for domestic manufacturing, slow permitting, restrict domestic mining including critical minerals, affect energy production, or inhibit capital formation, and its repeal recommendations would get a fast-track vote in Congress [S3]. Regulated industries would gain a dedicated channel to push for repeal of specific rules, with a task force dominated by 16 private-sector appointees chosen by the four congressional leaders [S3]. Small businesses would gain a guaranteed seat on the task force — at least 2 of the 4 appointees from each party leader must represent a small business — and a public portal to submit complaints about burdensome rules [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries, especially mining and energy

how_it_helps.text: Creates a task force of 18 members, 16 of them from the private sector and appointed by the four congressional party leaders, to identify federal regulations and guidance that burden U.S. industries and recommend their modification, consolidation, harmonization, or repeal.
Targets rules that inhibit competition, raise manufacturing costs, slow permitting, restrict domestic mining of critical minerals, affect energy production, or inhibit capital formation.

Gives repeal recommendations a fast-track path: each year OMB would send Congress a special message listing rules recommended for repeal, and a joint resolution repealing any of them would be discharged from committee after 25 days, get limited debate, bar amendments, and waive Senate points of order — a structure modeled on the Congressional Review Act.

Solicits public recommendations through a website, regulations.gov, and mail, publishes every submission in the Federal Register, and requires at least 2 small-business representatives among each party leader's appointees.

analysis.who_pays: The public would pay through the erosion of any repealed federal rules: weaker worker-safety, environmental, consumer, and financial protections would shift costs from businesses onto ordinary people in the form of dirtier air and water, riskier workplaces and products, and less recourse when harmed. Taxpayers would also fund the task force work through existing OMB budgets [S3].

drawbacks.text: The repeal process is one-way: the task force only identifies rules for modification or repeal, with no parallel process to strengthen rules that fall short, and the fast-track resolution path is available only for repeals — rules would only be able to get weaker, not stronger.

A private-sector majority (16 of 18 members) chosen by congressional leaders would effectively decide which public protections get recommended for repeal, with no requirement that public-health, labor, or consumer representatives hold seats.
Weaker rules shift real costs onto the public: more pollution, riskier workplaces and products, and less recourse for people harmed — savings for regulated industries are often costs borne elsewhere.

A fair objection in its favor: many federal rules do impose genuine compliance costs, slow permitting, and barriers for startups and small firms, and a structured review with public comment is a legitimate way to find and fix outdated rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — lower compliance costs, faster permitting, and easier market entry for businesses — come almost entirely from weakening the same federal rules that protect workers, consumers, and the environment, and its fast-track mechanism is designed to make repeal easy while offering no path to strengthen rules. The one-sided design, combined with a private-sector-majority task force, means the costs would fall on the public while the gains go to regulated industries. A modest plus is the public-comment process and guaranteed small-business representation, but these do not offset the structural one-way ratchet.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 7, 2022, and read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day.
No further action was taken; the committee never reported the bill, held no vote, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Support was limited: 6 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, all from the same party, and no House companion action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyday people are better off than under an enacted version, because the federal rules now on the books — covering worker safety, the environment, consumers, and finance — stayed in place. Regulated industries that hoped for a repeal pipeline gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing rules stayed in place; industries gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee of Utah
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Gary Peters, D)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, letting it die when the 117th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; sponsorship was entirely Republican, with 6 of 50 Senate Republicans cosponsoring and no Democratic support on record.

industries.note: The task force would target rules that restrict domestic mining, including critical minerals, and its repeal recommendations would get a fast-track vote in Congress. Rules repealed this way could include environmental and land protections that mining communities bear the costs of losing.

The bill directs the task force to evaluate rules that impact energy production or make the U.S. dependent on foreign energy, putting energy regulations in line for repeal recommendations. Weakening energy rules could shift pollution and safety costs onto the public.

The bill explicitly targets rules that increase operating costs and compliance burdens for domestic manufacturers, giving them a formal channel to seek repeal. Lower compliance costs for manufacturers can come at the price of weaker safety, labor, and environmental standards.

Small businesses are guaranteed representation on the task force and a portal to flag burdensome rules, and lighter compliance costs would help them. But the same repeal mechanism could strip rules that protect small firms as sellers, workers, and consumers.
